items.title: 7.2.2 Measuring the rate of a chemical reaction

source_refs.note: Topic 7.2.2, printed pages 147-148 (Table 7.1 and Figure 7.2), as printed, with Quick Check 7.3.

blocks.text: The measurement of rate of a chemical reaction involves the determination of the concentration of reactants or products at regular time intervals as the reaction progresses.

blocks.caption: Table 7.1 Change in concentration of HI with regular intervals, 2HI(g) → H₂(g) + I₂(g)

blocks.text: To determine the rate of reaction for a given length of time, a graph is plotted between time on x-axis and concentration of a reactant on y-axis, whereby a curve is obtained. To illustrate it, let us investigate the decomposition of HI to H₂ and I₂ at 500°C. By using the data, a graph is plotted as shown in Fig (7.3). The graph is between time on x-axis and concentration of HI in mol dm⁻³ on y-axis. Since HI is a reactant, so it is a falling curve. The steepness of the concentration-time curve reflects the progress of reaction. Greater the slope of curve near the start of reaction, greater is the rate of reaction.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: The graph of these data is Figure 7.2 (below); Figure 7.3 is the colorimetry picture in 7.2.3.

In order to measure the rate of reaction, draw a tangent say, at 100 seconds, on the curve and measure the slope of that tangent. The slope of the tangent is the rate of reaction at that point i.e., after 100 seconds. A right-angled triangle ABC is completed with a tangent as hypotenuse. Figure 7.2 shows that in 100 sec, the change in concentration is 0.04 mol dm⁻³. The rate is then calculated by using the following expression.

blocks.alt: Grid graph of [HI] (0 to 0.10 mol dm-3) against Time (s) (0 to 350). A green falling curve passes through yellow data points at 50 to 350 s, from 0.10 at the start. A blue tangent touches the curve at 100 s and runs from 0.08 at the y-axis to below 0.04. A right-angled triangle ABC: vertical leg from A at 0.08 down to C at 0.04 on the y-axis, labelled 0.04 mol dm-3, and horizontal leg from C to B on the tangent at about 164 s.
blocks.caption: Figure 7.2: The change in the HI concentration with time to the reaction 2HI(g) to H2(g) + I2(g) at 508 degrees C (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 7.2).

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Figure 7.2 the tangent falls by 0.04 mol dm⁻³ (A to C) over about 160 s (C to B), not 100 s; 100 s is only where the tangent touches the curve. The printed Figure 7.2 also labels the y-axis '[H1]' and puts the letter X on the vertical axis and Y on the horizontal one; the axis is [HI], with Y vertical and X horizontal, as drawn above.

blocks.text_alt: rate = 0.04 mol dm⁻³ / 100 sec = 4×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

blocks.text: This value of rate means that the concentration of HI is decreasing by 2.5 moles per dm⁻³ every second during the given interval.

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In Figure 7.2 the tangent falls by 0.04 mol dm⁻³ over about 160 s (the base CB of the triangle), not 100 s, so the rate at 100 s is 0.04 / 160 = about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (Table 7.1 gives a similar 2.6 × 10⁻⁴ around 100 s). The HI concentration is falling by about 2.5 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³, not 2.5 moles per dm³, every second.

If we plot a graph between time on x-axis and concentration of any of the products i.e H₂ or I₂, then a rising curve is obtained. The value of the tangent at 100 seconds will give the same value of rate of reaction as 4×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
book_errors: the same value of rate of reaction as 4×10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹

blocks.title: Book correction
blocks.text: In 2HI → H₂ + I₂, two moles of HI give one mole each of H₂ and I₂, so the tangent to the H₂ or I₂ curve at 100 s is half as steep as the HI tangent: about 1.3 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (half of 2.5 × 10⁻⁴), not the same value and not 4 × 10⁻⁴.

blocks.prompt: a) Plot the data in Table 7.1 for HI.
blocks.explanation: Plot time (x-axis) against [HI] (y-axis): the seven points of Table 7.1, from 0.100 mol dm⁻³ at 0 s to 0.0296 mol dm⁻³ at 300 s, lie on a smooth falling curve. (The diagram also shows the tangent used in part b.)

answer_figure.alt: Graph of Table 7.1: x-axis time 0–400 s, y-axis [HI] 0–0.10 mol dm⁻³. Seven orange points (0.100 at 0 s to 0.0296 at 300 s) lie on a green falling curve. A blue tangent at the 300 s point, with a triangle: Δc = 0.014 mol dm⁻³ (200 s to 400 s), Δt = 200 s. Box: rate = 0.014 / 200 = 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: graph of the HI data of Table 7.1 and the rate at 300 s from a tangent
answer_figure.long_description: The seven points of Table 7.1 (0, 50, 100, 150, 200, 250 and 300 s) are plotted and joined by a smooth falling curve. At 300 s (concentration 0.0296, about 0.03 mol dm⁻³) a tangent is drawn that touches the curve at only one point. Using the tangent as the hypotenuse of a triangle: from 200 s to 400 s (Δt = 200 s) the concentration falls by 0.014 mol dm⁻³. Rate = slope = 0.014 / 200 = 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

blocks.prompt: b) Calculate the rate after 300 sec (when the concentration is 0.03 mol dm⁻³) by drawing a tangent.
blocks.explanation: Draw the tangent at 300 s (0.0296 mol dm⁻³). Between 200 s and 400 s (Δt = 200 s) the concentration on the tangent falls by 0.014 mol dm⁻³, so rate = 0.014 / 200 = 7.0 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (about 7 × 10⁻⁵). The average from 250 s to 300 s (0.0040 / 50 = 8 × 10⁻⁵) comes out slightly higher, because it is a straight line joining two points, not a tangent.

blocks.prompt: c) Use the same method to calculate the rate of reaction at HI concentrations of 0.10 mol dm⁻³, 0.050 mol dm⁻³ and 0.02 mol dm⁻³.
blocks.explanation: Draw the tangent to the curve at each concentration and find its slope. At 0.10 mol dm⁻³ (t = 0) the tangent is steepest: it falls 0.040 mol dm⁻³ in 50 s, rate = 0.040 / 50 = 8.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹ (about 8 × 10⁻⁴). At 0.050 mol dm⁻³ (about 125 s) the tangent falls 0.040 in 200 s, rate = 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. 0.02 mol dm⁻³ lies beyond Table 7.1 (which ends at 300 s); extending the curve (to about 500 s), the tangent gives a rate of about 3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.

answer_figure.alt: [HI] against time (0–550 s): the Table 7.1 points on a green curve, dashed beyond 300 s (extended). Three tangents: red at 0.10 (t = 0), triangle Δt = 50 s, Δc = 0.040; blue at 0.050 (about 125 s), triangle Δt = 200 s, Δc = 0.040; dark blue at 0.02 (about 500 s). Box with the rates: 8.0 × 10⁻⁴, 2.0 × 10⁻⁴ and about 3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹.
answer_figure.caption: Answer diagram: rates from tangents at [HI] = 0.10, 0.050 and 0.02 mol dm⁻³
answer_figure.long_description: The Table 7.1 curve is extended beyond 300 s by a dashed line so that it reaches 0.02 mol dm⁻³. At the start (0.10) the red tangent is steepest: in its triangle the concentration falls 0.040 mol dm⁻³ in 50 s, rate 8.0 × 10⁻⁴. At 0.050 the blue tangent is less steep: a fall of 0.040 in 200 s, rate 2.0 × 10⁻⁴. At 0.02 the dark blue tangent is almost flat, rate about 3 × 10⁻⁵ mol dm⁻³ s⁻¹. The lower the concentration, the flatter the tangent and the lower the rate.

blocks.prompt: d) What do you deduce about the rate of the reaction with time from these calculations?
blocks.explanation: As time passes the concentration falls and the rate of the reaction keeps decreasing.

blocks.prompt: e) At which concentration, the rate is highest, and lowest?
blocks.explanation: The rate is highest at 0.10 mol dm⁻³ and lowest at 0.02 mol dm⁻³.
